narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated an 88.3% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a very high risk estimate, not a certainty, but the university used it to conclude that admitting you would be too risky under its rules. The strongest signal was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This sharply increased the predicted failure risk. The second strongest signal was your first-year class standing, also in the lowest decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile; it likewise pushed the prediction toward failure. Third, your LSAT score of 32 was below the accepted-student average of about 37, adding further risk. Your gender and race were not used in the decision. Next, ask admissions whether you can appeal or receive feedback, and consider retaking the LSAT with preparation. Meet an academic advisor to address the weak class-standing pattern, and apply to programs that review applicants holistically. If you can show improvement, updated scores, or strong supporting circumstances, you may strengthen a future application.
